question.text: This brother of Hu´ascar and last Incan Emperor was captured by Francisco Pizarro at the Battle of Cajamarca [kah-hah-MAR-kah]. This emperor was executed despite paying a room's worth of gold for his ransom.
question.clue: He offered to fill a large room with gold and silver for his ransom, but the Spaniards didn't release him.

swap.leadin: These people stored numerical information by using colored and knotted strings called quipus (KEE-poos).
swap.text: Name these people who also communicated using an extensive road network in the Andes called the "royal road" in Quechua (KEH-choo-uh). Their empire included sites like Machu Picchu (MAH-choo PEEK-choo) in modern-day Peru.
swap.clue: Descendants of this empire's royalty included Garcilaso de la Vega, and this empire was sometimes named for the four administrative suyus that it was divided into.

question.leadin: Answer the following about indigenous peoples of South America.
question.text: The Quechua group, who share their name with the language of the Inca Empire, live in and around this mountain range in Peru, Ecuador, and Bolivia.
question.clue: A culture in this mountain range depicted a spider called the "Decapitator" and created a mummy known as the Lord of Sipan.

swap.text: Identify the Spaniard who conquered the Incan Empire.
swap.clue: This man received help from longtime partner Diego Almagro, but he was killed by Almagro's forces in the Battle of Las Salinas.

question.text: Paul Kosok discovered the Hummingbird, an earthwork built by these people indigenous to Peru. These people built the city of Cahuachi [ca-WA-chee] and used puquios to irrigate their crops.
question.clue: Paul Kosok and Maria Reiche (RAI-keh) mapped structures created by these people.

swap.leadin: This empire used multicolored strings of knots known as quipu to send long-distance messages.
swap.text: First, name this empire in modern-day Peru, whose capital of Cuzco was sacked by the Spanish under Pizarro.
swap.clue: After the Battle of Cajamarca , Atahualpa was captured and executed by Francisco Pizarro, ending this polity.

question.text: Cusco was the capital of this South American empire.
question.clue: This empire's capital city, Cuzco, was captured by the conquistador Francisco Pizarro.

swap.text: The mita was used by Spanish rulers to obtain a labor force for this largest silver mine in the Spanish Empire, in which thousands died from mercury poisoning. It lies in present-day Bolivia.
swap.clue: Workers in this city still give offerings to a goat-headed underworld deity called "The Uncle" or El Tio.

question.text: The Shining Path began its operations from the Andean region of this country. This nation contains the site of Machu Picchu.
question.clue: The second half of A Fish in the Water is a memoir by a candidate for this country's presidency, whose FREDEMO coalition lost to a man supported by APRA and Cambio 90.

swap.text: This Spaniard was the subject of an unflattering history by Agustin de Zarate. This rival of Diego de Almagro ordered the execution of a captive despite having received a ransom of a room filled with gold and silver.
swap.clue: Gonzalo also led a revolt against Blasco Nunez Vela for attempting to enforce the New Laws under Charles V. Another man with this surname served under Balboa and briefly served as mayor of Panama City.

question.text: Incan relay messengers, the chasquis, carried messages via these "talking knots" that were made of llama hair.
question.clue: This objects that were used for record-keeping and other purposes by the Inca.

swap.leadin: Part of these people's confederation was ruled by a zipa, who would cover his body in gold dust and jump into Lake Guatavita along with some gold offerings.
swap.text: Name these people, whose confederation was ruled by a zipa in the south and a zaque in the north. The last powerful cacique of these people, Tundama, was killed with a large hammer by Balthasar Maldonado.
swap.clue: This confederation of Northern Andean tribes that was led by co-rulers called Zipa and Zaque. They were encountered by the Conquistador Gonzalo Jimenez de Quesada after his expedition sailed up the Magdalena.

question.leadin: Helaine Silverman labels Site 165 as this culture's "urban" capital, in contrast to a "religious" capital that contains a "Room of Posts."
question.text: Name this culture located around the Ingenio Valley, which evolved from the Paracas culture according to Silverman. This Peruvian culture created puquios to irrigate terraces at sites like Cahuachi.
question.clue: This culture built the Cantalloc ("cahn-TAH-yoke")Aqueducts, exemplifying the corkscrew entrances of their puquios ("poo-KEE-ohʼs").

swap.text: Vilcabamba was founded by this Incan monarch. This monarch was captured by Spanish forces and imprisoned by the brothers of Francisco Pizarro before escaping and laying siege to Cusco for 10 months.

question.leadin: Name some mythical places sought by Spanish explorers.
question.text: Legends of this city originated with the Muisca people of Colombia, whose chiefs supposedly covered themselves in gold dust. Pizarro and Orellana's search for this city led to the discovery of the Amazon River.
question.clue: During the first part of the journey in which Orellana travelled the length of the Amazon, a valley of Cinnamon and this place were the targets of Gonzalo Pizzaro.

swap.leadin: After being attacked by the rival Chanka people, this ruler is said to have called on the sun god Inti to turn stones into pururauca warriors to defend his city.
swap.text: Name this son of Viracocha who transformed the Kingdom of Cuzco into the Incan Empire in the 15th century.
swap.clue: This king commissioned life-sized gold statues of animals and plant for the central garden of his Coricancha temple.

question.text: The original "Maritime Foundations" theory was developed after the excavation of this site at the mouth of the Supe River that likely provided fish to Caral from the nearby ocean. This place is the type site of the Norte Chico.

swap.leadin: This cloud forest culture created mosaic friezes at Gran Pajaten ("pa-ha-TEN"), built cliff tombs at Revash, and produced the Laguna de Los Condores textiles.
swap.text: Name this culture that built the walled city of Kuelap in Amazonas, Peru. This culture's people were ascribed white skin by Inca chroniclers, whose reports of their ferocity inspired their nickname of "warriors of the clouds."

question.leadin: Andy Watkins is a peasant in the Incan empire. Name some stuff about Andy's life.
question.text: Andy is in Chan Chan and wants to tell his friends in Panchacamac about how much he loves e.e. cummings. He will have to solicit a chasqui messenger along the extensive Incan road system, who will store the information on one of these braided "talking knots."
question.clue: Evidence for a writing system in these objects include a three-number sequence possibly representing the village of Puruchuco (poo-roo-CHOO-koh).

swap.leadin: John Rick analyzed the acoustics of the central building in this place, noting that it was designed to encourage a feeling of sounds coming from every direction at once.
swap.text: Identify this archaeological site in Peru, where religious rituals took place as early as 1200 BCE. The only entrance to the Old Temple at this site faced the Mosna River to the east.
swap.clue: This site, which was excavated by Julio C. Tello ("TAY-yo") and is located east of the Cordillera ("cor-di-YEH-ra") Blanca. This site was the centre of a namesake culture which domesticated camelids.
